data.title: Causes, Educational Losses, and State Response

data.heading: Roots of Forced Child Labor
bullets: According to ILRF study 'We Live Subject to Their Orders' (2008)
Roots are not poverty or tradition, but the nature of the state
Command economy with quotas and demechanization
Machine harvesting fell from two-thirds to 10%
Mobilization of children through schools organized by khokimiats

narr: The ILRF study 'We Live Subject to Their Orders' (2008) reveals important insights into the roots of forced child labor.
Contrary to assumptions, the roots are not poverty or tradition, but rather the nature of the state system.
The command economy with strict quotas and demechanization created the need for forced labor.
Machine harvesting dramatically decreased from two-thirds to just 10%.
The mobilization of children was systematically organized through schools by local authorities (khokimiats).

Two months of school closures represented a loss of over 20% of instructional time.
For students in grades 5-9, these accumulated losses amounted to a full academic year over time.
This educational disruption had profound long-term consequences for children's development.

narr: Over time, the state began to respond to these issues.
In 2001, cotton harvesting was officially included in the list of worst forms of child labor.
In March 2008, the parliament pledged to ratify ILO conventions No. 182 and No. 138.
These conventions were ratified in March 2008 and March 2009 respectively.
The 2007 Law 'On Guarantees of the Child's Right to Labor' established age limits for work.
It permits work from age 16, age 15 with written parental consent, and age 14 for light work outside of school.

data.heading: Question 1 — Definition of Forced Labor
data.problem: How does ILO Convention No. 29 define forced labor?
steps: The definition includes all work or service exacted from any person
This must be under the threat of any penalty
The person must not have offered themselves voluntarily
Four key elements: work/service, any person, involuntary nature, threat of punishment
data.result: Forced labor means 'all work or service which is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty and to which he has not offered himself voluntarily.'

narr: Let's start with the fundamental definition of forced labor according to ILO Convention No. 29.
The definition includes all work or service that is exacted from any person.
This must occur under the threat of some penalty.
Crucially, the person must not have offered themselves voluntarily.
These four elements together define forced labor in international law.

data.heading: Question 2 — Cases for Immediate Cessation
data.problem: In what five cases does Convention No. 105 require the immediate cessation of forced labor?
steps: As a means of political coercion or education
As punishment for political opinions
As a method for economic development
As a means of ensuring labor discipline
As punishment for participation in strikes
As a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination
data.result: Convention No. 105 requires immediate cessation of forced labor in five specific cases: political coercion/education/opinions, economic development, labor discipline, strike participation, and discrimination.

narr: While Convention No. 29 prohibits forced labor in general with some exceptions,
Convention No. 105 requires its immediate cessation in five specific cases.
First, as a means of political coercion or education.
Second, as punishment for political opinions.
Third, as a method for economic development.
Fourth, as a means of ensuring labor discipline.
Fifth, as punishment for participation in strikes.
Sixth, as a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination.

data.result: Uzbekistan has ratified 17 ILO conventions including No. 29, 105, 182, 138, and the 2014 Protocol to No. 29, plus the 1966 UN Covenants.

narr: Uzbekistan has ratified several key ILO conventions.
As of January 1, 2021, it had ratified 17 conventions (including 8 fundamental ones) and 1 protocol.
These include Convention No. 29 (1930) and No. 105 (1957) specifically on forced labor.
Also Convention No. 182 (1999) on worst forms of child labor.
And Convention No. 138 (1973) on minimum age for work.
The 2014 Protocol to Convention No. 29 was ratified on June 25, 2019.
Additionally, Uzbekistan has ratified the 1966 UN Covenants.

The country has a complex relationship with cotton production that historically involved widespread child labor.
